question: According to the Japanese daily Nikkei Asia1, the Chinese state-owned company China National Electronics Import & Export Corporation (CEIEC) is involved in the construction in Belarus of a production line for 122 mm rocket warhead components. The contract with the Belarusian state-owned ZTEM plant (Precise Electro-Mechanics Plant) was signed in December 2023.

It includes the design and supply of equipment, technical documentation and the training of personnel. The new line is intended to produce warhead components for 122 mm rockets (including the filling stage for TNT-type explosives) – exactly the type of ammunition that Russia is using on a huge scale in its war against Ukraine (BM-21 Grad and similar systems).

The planned production capacity is equivalent to around 120 000 missiles per year once the production line is fully operational. Production is scheduled to start in the second half of 2026. Chinese specialists are to oversee the production of the first 500 units and then train the Belarusian personnel. The specifications described in the media indicate that the weapons will be intended for export to Russia.
This is yet another sign of China’s real support for Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. 1.
Is the EU aware of China’s cooperation with Belarus in the production of ammunition for offensive military systems?
Is the EU aware of the scale of China’s involvement in arms and ammunition production in Russia and Belarus? What action does it intend to take against Beijing?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.4.2026) The Commission is aware of the information referenced by the Honourable Member. The Commission continuously monitors developments that may contribute to Russia’s ability to sustain its war of aggression against Ukraine.

Where credible information emerges regarding activities that may circumvent or undermine existing EU restrictive measures (sanctions), the Commission engages on the matter carefully together with Member States as well as with relevant third countries.

The EU has adopted an extensive set of individual and sectoral sanctions – across 19 packages – in response to Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, including measures targeting Russia’s military industrial complex and entities involved in supporting it1. The EU also maintains sanctions against Belarus for its role in facilitating Russia’s aggression.

The EU continues to engage with China at all levels, calling on China to stop any support which directly or indirectly strengthens Russia’s military capabilities. To this date, the EU has taken different restrictive measures against more than 100 Chinese companies and individuals supporting Russia’s war effort.

The Commission and the High Representative/Vice-President will continue to monitor the situation closely and propose additional measures where necessary to safeguard the effectiveness of EU sanctions and to address any activities that contribute to Russia’s ability to wage its war against Ukraine.
